meta.estate: Layered estate — EU service on foreign technology

meta.title: Cloud Sovereignty Self-Assessment — Deep-Analysis Teaching Workbook

frontSheet: This is the deep-analysis teaching workbook: it exists to prove that the technical-dimensions diagram in the EC implementation guidance (p.12, 'Depth of analysis') is fully expressible in this model. Every block on that diagram becomes a dimension, every layer box a stratum, and the Development block's Software Supplier / Service Provider boxes become party types on the second axis.

The two objectives mirror the EC's own split of its 43 deep-analysis questions: 9 target the legal entities in the chain (here DEEP-ENT, party grain — 'the evaluation must not stop at the level of the legal entity which applied to the tender'), 19 are asked per relevant entity across the technical dimensions (here DEEP-TEC, dimension grain over all nine diagram dimensions).

Nesting rule, taught twice: when a two-deep block shares one control fact across its leaves, it flattens into strata — Security becomes siem-service, siem-software, threat, xdr-edr under a single question. When sibling sub-blocks ask different facts, each gets its own question on a shared dimension — Containers, PaaS are two questions on the one platform dimension. No third structural level is ever needed.

The critical set is the EC's own foundation list — compute, storage, network, security, IAM, critical PaaS. Edge (the Advanced block), software supply (Development), facilities (Power, Estate) score without ever gating the floor.

Expected ceiling, per the EC lessons-learnt: SEAL-3+ stays out of reach while the hardware, chips strata depend on non-EU supply. The third test estate demonstrates it — an all-EU chain that still floors at SEAL-2.
Don't know is an honest answer. It never counts as zero; the floor is always reported together with its unknown count, so a guess is worse than an admission.

sealLevels.name: No Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Service, technology or operations under exclusive control of non-EU third parties, governed entirely by non-EU jurisdictions.

sealLevels.name: Jurisdictional Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU law formally applies with limited practical enforceability; control can still be overridden from outside the EU.

sealLevels.name: Data Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU jurisdictions apply and the EU controls the data even under stress; material dependencies on non-EU parties remain.

sealLevels.name: Technological Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU actors exercise meaningful control over the technology and can keep operating if a foreign supplier withdraws.

sealLevels.name: Full Digital Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Technology and operations under complete EU control, subject only to EU jurisdiction, with no critical non-EU dependencies.

roles.name: Architecture
roles.description: Designs the estate; owns topology and platform choices.

roles.name: Platform ops
roles.description: Runs the estate day to day.

roles.name: Security
roles.description: Owns controls, identity, and incident response.

roles.name: Legal
roles.description: Owns contracts, jurisdiction, and data-protection law.

roles.name: Procurement
roles.description: Owns supplier selection, exit, and commercial terms.

roles.name: Facilities
roles.description: Owns the physical estate: power, cooling, buildings, physical access.

parties.name: Institution
parties.description: The assessed party — the estate owner (EC: Contracting Authority).

parties.name: Service provider
parties.description: Delivers, operates cloud services for the estate — the diagram's Service Provider box.

parties.name: Sub-contractor
parties.description: A legal entity involved in the delivery of the contract, under the provider (EC footnote 1).

parties.name: Supplier
parties.description: Delivers hardware or software without unsupervised access to the infrastructure — the diagram's Software Supplier box (EC footnote 2).

questions.text: Can the institution name every legal entity involved in delivering this estate, down to hardware, software suppliers?
questions.why: Deep analysis must not stop at the legal entity that signed the contract — the EC's own rule. The chain has to be enumerated before any of it can be assessed, so this single assessment-axis question is the precondition for every party-axis answer that follows.

ladder.description: Only the contract-signing entity is known; nobody could list who actually delivers the service.
Sub-contractors named in the contract are known; the suppliers behind them are not.
Every sub-contractor is enumerated; hardware, software suppliers are mapped for the critical dimensions.
Every sub-contractor, supplier is enumerated per dimension; the map is refreshed at each contract change.
The full chain is enumerated down to the layer it serves; audit rights reach every entity on it.

questions.text: Under which jurisdiction does this party ultimately operate?
questions.why: The Development block draws Software Supplier, Service Provider as boxes inside the estate — but they are parties, not layers: the same jurisdiction question walks the whole chain on the party axis, because a sovereign service resting on a compellable supplier is not sovereign.

ladder.description: Non-EU jurisdiction reaches this party directly; disclosure or shutdown can be ordered today.
An EU entity signs the contract; ultimate ownership answers to a non-EU jurisdiction.
EU law governs this party; named non-EU dependencies remain inside its own supply chain.
This party, including its controlling owners, sits wholly under EU/EEA jurisdiction.
The whole ownership chain is EU-domiciled; no foreign order has a lawful path to this party.

questions.text: Who could keep this dimension running if every non-EU party withdrew tomorrow?
questions.why: The diagram gives Compute, Storage, Network the same four layer boxes — Service, Software, Hardware, Chips — because the honest answer differs by layer. One question fans over all three dimensions; a workshop splits any of them into strata the moment a sovereign-run service turns out to sit on foreign silicon.

ladder.description: Under exclusive non-EU control; a withdrawal stops this outright, no EU actor can step in.
EU actors operate it under non-EU licences, support, updates that can be revoked from outside.
EU-controlled operation; replacement or repair still needs named non-EU technology.
EU actors control operation, source, deployment; a non-EU withdrawal is a planned, tested event.
Built, run, replaceable entirely under EU control; no non-EU dependency remains.

questions.text: Under whose control does this part of IAM operate?
questions.why: IAM's layer boxes are not the canonical four — the diagram names Identity, Access. Strata are author-named per dimension, so the split follows the diagram: the identity store can be sovereign while access decisions ride a foreign policy engine, or the reverse.

ladder.description: A non-EU provider's system is authoritative; it can lock the estate out or mint access on its own.
The authoritative system runs under EU control; recovery or federation still routes through a non-EU provider.
Identity records, access decisions run on EU-controlled systems; no outside party can grant or revoke anything.

questions.text: Who controls the container platform the estate's workloads run on?
questions.why: Platform Management holds three sub-blocks. IAM became its own dimension; Containers, PaaS stay in one platform dimension asking different facts — one question per sub-block, sharing the service, software strata. The alternative — flattening — is what the security dimension demonstrates.

ladder.description: Workloads run only on a non-EU managed service; no self-hosted path exists.
Self-hosted on a non-EU distribution; images, patches arrive solely from that vendor.
EU-operated platform on foreign-governed open source; the estate builds its own images from source.
EU-operated on an EU-maintained distribution; upstream is a contribution, not a dependency.
Platform, distribution, build chain sit under EU control end to end.

questions.text: Who controls the PaaS services — databases, queues, runtimes — the estate depends on?
questions.why: The EC's critical-services list ends with 'critical PaaS services': PaaS is the layer where proprietary APIs quietly re-attach an estate to a foreign stack after every layer below has been made sovereign.

ladder.description: Proprietary non-EU PaaS APIs with no compatible alternative; the workloads cannot move.
Non-EU PaaS behind open APIs; migration is asserted, never exercised.
EU-operated PaaS on non-EU software under an open licence.
EU-operated PaaS on EU-maintained software; a migration off it has been exercised.
PaaS built, operated, evolved under EU control; no non-EU service sits in the path.

questions.text: Under whose effective control does this security capability operate?
questions.why: The Security block nests two deep — SIEM splits into Service, Software while Threat, XDR/EDR are single boxes. The model needs no third structural level: the block flattens into one honest stratum list (siem-service, siem-software, threat, xdr-edr), because a single control fact — who runs it, who sees the telemetry — spans all four leaves.

ladder.description: A non-EU party operates it; telemetry leaves EU jurisdiction; it can be disabled from outside.
EU-operated on non-EU tooling whose vendor keeps remote access to the data it processes.
EU-operated under EU jurisdiction; detection content, updates arrive from non-EU sources.
EU-operated, EU-governed tooling; non-EU feeds are an input, never a dependency.
Runs entirely under EU control; logs, alerts, response never leave EU jurisdiction.

questions.text: Who controls the software factory that builds, signs, releases the estate's software?
questions.why: The Development block's Software Factory has its own Service, Software boxes — a hosted pipeline is a service dependency, the build tooling a software one. Whoever holds the pipeline, the signing keys decides what ships.

ladder.description: Builds run on a non-EU hosted service that also holds the signing keys.
Builds run under EU control on non-EU tooling; signing keys never leave the estate.
Pipeline, tooling, signing sit under EU control; a release needs no non-EU system.

questions.text: Could the estate keep building its software if access to upstream libraries, frameworks were cut?
questions.why: Libraries / Frameworks is the diagram's reminder that open source is also a supply chain: an estate that cannot build without foreign registries has a dependency no contract governs.

ladder.description: Every build pulls straight from non-EU registries; a cut-off stops builds the same day.
A local cache exists as a side effect; nobody has proven a build succeeds from it alone.
A curated EU-hosted mirror serves every build; provenance is recorded for critical components.
Dependencies are vendored or mirrored with verified provenance; an air-gapped build has been run.
Every dependency is mirrored, provenance-verified, rebuildable from source under EU control.

questions.text: Who controls the edge protection standing in front of the estate?
questions.why: The Advanced block's DDoS, CDN boxes are the strata here: one control fact — who stands in front of the front door — with truth that routinely differs, EU scrubbing behind a non-EU CDN being the classic split. Edge sits outside the EC's foundation list, so this dimension scores without ever gating.

ladder.description: A non-EU service terminates the estate's traffic; it can inspect or drop that traffic at will.
A non-EU service fronts the estate under contract terms forbidding inspection; enforcement is contractual only.
An EU-operated service fronts the estate; attack surge capacity is rented from a non-EU network.
EU-operated, EU-owned capacity absorbs attack load; a non-EU fallback engages only on the institution's decision.
Every point of presence runs on EU-controlled infrastructure.

questions.text: Who controls this physical layer of the facilities the estate stands on?
questions.why: The diagram's bottom row — Power, the Estate's Cooling, Building — grounds the whole picture: deep analysis reaches the ground the racks stand on, so the physical world gets a dimension with three strata like any other.

ladder.description: Owned, operated by a non-EU party; physical access is theirs to grant.
EU-operated; maintenance, spare parts for this layer come from non-EU suppliers.
Owned, operated, maintainable under EU control; physical access is EU-decided end to end.

testEstates.name: Everything under one non-EU roof
testEstates.description: The diagram collapsed: one hyperscale provider serves all nine dimensions, so the exposure map shows a single party standing under the entire estate. Deep analysis finds nothing to split — every layer answers 0 or 1 and the floor is SEAL-0 across both objectives.

testEstates.name: EU-run service on foreign technology
testEstates.description: The pattern deep analysis exists to expose: an EU provider runs the service layer while hardware, chips, edge, libraries stay foreign — with a hardware supplier and a security sub-contractor standing in the chain exactly the way the Development block draws them. All four party types appear. Whole-dimension answers throughout; a live workshop would split compute into strata instead of averaging down to 1.

testEstates.name: EU chain, foreign silicon
testEstates.description: The lessons-learnt estate: an EU cooperative runs every layer, the factory signs its own releases, the whole chain answers at SEAL-3 — yet compute, storage, network answer 2 because the chips stratum is foreign, so the floor holds at SEAL-2. SEAL-3+ stays out of reach exactly as the EC's lessons-learnt predicts.

Runners are self-hosted; signing keys sit in the estate HSM; the pipeline service is non-EU.
EU scrubbing centre under contract; surge capacity is rented from a non-EU network.
Static assets terminate at CDN-Front's non-EU points of presence.
Supplier map exists for the six critical dimensions; last refreshed at contract renewal.
